LanceDB · Robotics · LeRobot

One table to train your robot: LanceDB as the data layer for robotics

We trained the same robot policies twice — once with stock LeRobot on its standard parquet+mp4 layout, once with the same mp4 bytes in Lance format — across two regimes: a fast ACT policy where the dataloader sets the pace, and a 450M vision-language-action model where it doesn't. Same pixels, same trained behavior, same size on disk. What changes: training wall-clock on realistic CPU budgets, and what your dataset can do when it's a real table.

2.31×
faster end-to-end DROID training at a 4-vCPU/GPU cloud budget (full 20k-step runs)
2.85×
training throughput at 3 vCPU/GPU — the dataloader-cost ceiling
82.0%
avg LIBERO success for the Lance-trained VLA (base: 80.8%)
13 ms
text → frame semantic search over 273k frames

Two systems glued together

Robot learning data is video plus a little bit of table: a few camera streams, proprioceptive state, actions, task strings. The standard LeRobot v3 format stores this as two systems — parquet for the tabular columns, chunked mp4 files for pixels — with bookkeeping metadata holding them together. Video is the right container for camera streams; the glue is where training hurts. A shuffled VLA batch with a 50-step action chunk means seeking into mp4s and decoding GOPs, sample after sample — and nothing about parquet+mp4 can answer a question like "show me every frame where the gripper is above the stove."

lerobot-lancedb collapses the two systems into one: a Lance table for the tabular columns and a companion blob v2 table holding the same mp4 bytes, verbatim. The dataset stays video-sized (1.9 GB for LIBERO's 273k frames), decoded pixels are bit-exact vs the source videos (we checked: max pixel diff 0.0), and the format supplies what the glue can't — fast frame-level random access, S3 byte-range streaming, and secondary indexes on the same table. Everything below is measured on a 4×H100 / 104-core box; every script is in the lancedb/training example.

Part 1 — Speed, measured honestly (ACT on DROID)

The speed test pairs a fast policy with real-robot data: ACT (~50M params) on DROID-100 — the DROID manipulation dataset as published for LeRobot (3 cameras per frame, 180×320). Identical 4×H100 trainings, same seed, same mp4 bytes; the only variable is the data layer and the CPU budget, which we pin per run (both backends treated identically) to emulate real machines:

The full 20k-step wall-clocks confirm the steady-state numbers: at 4 vCPU/GPU Lance finished in 50m04s vs 1h55m37s for base (2.31×); at 8 vCPU/GPU, 33m06s vs 60m37s (1.83×). Loss curves match to the third decimal at every logged step — same bytes, same model, same result; one just waits on its dataloader.

Why does the gap grow as CPU shrinks? Because the dataloader itself — measured in isolation, no training attached — is where the advantage lives, and training only exposes it when the loader is the binding constraint. Put the loader-only ratio next to the e2e ratio at each budget and you can watch the convergence:

read patternloader-only
(isolated, 8 wkr)		e2e @ 26
vCPU/GPU		e2e @ 8e2e @ 4e2e @ 3
DROID (3 cams)2.37×1.26×1.92×2.57×2.85×
ALOHA sim (1 cam, 480×640)2.81×1.06×1.29×2.31×2.47×

Abundant CPU hides the loader (right columns → 1×); squeeze it and the e2e number climbs to — and on DROID slightly past — the loader-only ratio, because a starved mp4 loader also steals CPU from the trainer's own threads. The generalization holds across datasets, and even at lerobot's stock defaults on the full 104-thread box (no CPU cap anywhere) the ALOHA run shows 1.46×. The ALOHA full 20k-step pair: 53 min (Lance) vs 99 min (base). The batch-size sweep (1.98×→2.31× when demand rises at fixed CPU) and all loader matrices are in the repro repo.

Faster GPUs make this gap bigger, not smaller

Every accelerator generation raises sample demand while CPU-per-GPU stays roughly flat (DGX H100 and DGX B200 ship the same ~14 cores/GPU). We measured the mechanism directly: raising demand at fixed CPU moved the delta from 1.98× to 2.31×. An H200 does to demand what a bigger batch does; a B200/B300 does much more. The budget-tier column of the chart is a preview of where faster GPUs take every configuration — the gap grows toward the dataloader-cost ceiling (~2.4–2.9× on these patterns). A ready-to-run H200/B300 runbook ships with the repo to verify this on newer silicon.

Where does the speed leg's quality proof come from? The ALOHA pair's checkpoints run in the gym-aloha simulator: 0% success before training; 60% (base-trained) vs 58% (Lance-trained) over 50 episodes each — a statistical tie, from checkpoints that took 99 vs 53 minutes to train.

Part 2 — Integration

The dataset classes are drop-in subclasses of LeRobotDataset — isinstance checks pass, EpisodeAwareSampler works, the language collate sees task strings. The standard integration, as in the plugin docs (and how the official LeRobot docs reference Lance-backed datasets), is to construct the dataset wherever your code builds one and hand it to your existing trainer:

from lerobot_lancedb import LeRobotLanceVideoDataset

dataset = LeRobotLanceVideoDataset(
    "lerobot/droid_100", root="./droid100_lance",
    delta_timestamps=delta_timestamps,   # resolved from your policy config as usual
    return_uint8=True,
)
# everything downstream is unchanged: EpisodeAwareSampler, DataLoader, your train loop

Converting an existing dataset is one command that finishes in seconds — the mp4 bytes are copied verbatim into the blob column, which is also why decoded frames are bit-exact (we checked: max pixel diff 0.0):

lerobot-convert-to-lance-video --repo-id=your/dataset --src-root=... --output=./ds_lance

Prefer the stock lerobot-train CLI with zero changes to your commands? lerobot's factory has no dataset-class hook, so the plugin-compatible constructor (v0.2+) lets a 7-line launcher point the factory at the Lance class — a pragmatic patch, clearly labeled as one:

# train_lance.py — keep the lerobot-train CLI, swap the storage
import lerobot.datasets.factory as factory
from lerobot_lancedb import LeRobotLanceVideoDataset

factory.LeRobotDataset = LeRobotLanceVideoDataset

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from lerobot.scripts.lerobot_train import main
    main()

Part 3 — VLA example: SmolVLA on LIBERO

The VLA leg of the example: SmolVLA (450M, language-conditioned) finetuned on the LIBERO benchmark with both backends — identical 40k-step recipes, task strings flowing through the language collate — evaluated closed-loop over all four suites, 100 episodes per suite per model. (No speed claims in this section: at 450M the GPU is the bottleneck and both formats keep it fed.)

Seeing is believing — same checkpoint, before and after:

"pick up the alphabet soup and place it in the basket"
"put both the cream cheese box and the butter in the basket"
An eval gotcha we hit so you don't have to: LeRobot's --policy.n_action_steps controls how much of SmolVLA's 50-step action chunk executes open-loop before re-planning — and it dominates measured success. The same checkpoint that scores 82% closed-loop scores 14.8% executing 10 steps per chunk. If your LIBERO numbers look inexplicably bad, check this flag before blaming your model.

Part 4 — Stream training data from S3

The Lance reader takes an s3:// URI directly — byte-range reads against the blob column, no local copy. Measured from a same-region bucket on the LIBERO table:

2,458/s
samples/s streaming from S3, 16 workers
1,445/s
at 8 workers
0 bytes
of local disk required

That is several times what the 4-GPU trainings above consume — object storage becomes a place you can train from, not just sync from. It matters most when the corpus outgrows the training node: Lance's random access means an episode list from a table query can train on a 50 GB slice of a 10 TB bucket without materializing the rest.

Part 5 — The training table is also a database

This is where the format decision compounds. Everything in this section ran against the exact table the trainer reads — no export, no copy, no second system.

Backfill features with Geneva

We added a SigLIP2 embedding column with Geneva, LanceDB's feature-engineering engine: a stateful, batched, GPU-scheduled UDF (the model loads once per worker; batches arrive as Arrow arrays) registered as a virtual column, then materialized by a distributed, checkpointed backfill job:

@udf(data_type=pa.list_(pa.float32(), 768), num_gpus=1, input_columns=["index"])
class EmbedAgentview:                      # stateful: SigLIP2 loads once per worker
    def __call__(self, index: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:   # batched
        # decodes pixels straight from the Lance video blob table
        ...

tbl.add_columns({"emb_image": EmbedAgentview(lance_root)})
tbl.backfill("emb_image", concurrency=2)   # 273,465 frames ≈ 10 min on 2 GPUs

Two things worth noticing. The UDF reads pixels from the video blob column — the frames table never stores image bytes. And the write is zero-copy schema evolution: a commit that adds a column, no rewrite of the 1.9 GB of video.

Four more things the same table answers

Near-duplicate episodes — embed once, then redundancy pruning is a matrix product: comparing mid-episode frames across all 1,693 episodes takes 0.9 s and surfaces episode pair (1106, 1210) at >0.995 cosine similarity — drop one before training:

Outlier mining — within a task, frames farthest from the task's visual centroid are your teleop glitches and camera-occlusion moments: episode 217 shows up twice in the top-5 anomalies for the microwave tasks — the arm swallowing the lens, exactly the frames to eyeball before they pollute a finetune:

Hybrid queries — full-text and vector compose: "the gripper is holding the object in the air" restricted to task LIKE '%basket%' answers in 25 ms, turning "find me mid-grasp frames in basket tasks" into one call.

Time travel — every schema evolution and backfill committed a table version (this table has 26). lance.dataset(uri, version=N) re-opens the exact table a run trained on — reproducible splits without manifest files.

Close the loop: curation → training split

Curation only matters if it feeds back into training. Here a SQL filter on the task column becomes an episode list becomes a finetune — zero bytes copied:

eps = tbl.search().where(f"task IN ({object_tasks})") \
         .select(["episode_index"]).to_pandas()["episode_index"].unique()
# → 454 episodes, 66,984 frames; feed straight into --dataset.episodes

What the curated split actually trained

We ran the finetune. From 0% to 77% on its suite in 10k steps (~35 minutes of training) — the entire "dataset" was a SQL query. The table's honesty keeps paying: the 20k and 30k checkpoints decline to 76% and 72% — 454 episodes overfit fast, and you catch it because every checkpoint pairs with a versioned, reproducible split. The 40-task generalist still wins the suite at 89%: at this scale multi-task transfer beats a narrow finetune, and learning that costs exactly one query and one training run when curation lives in the data layer.

Why this works: blob v2, in one paragraph

The video table stores each mp4's raw bytes in a large_binary column whose field metadata (lance-encoding:blob=true) turns on Lance's blob encoding: values live in blob-oriented data files, the column materializes as lightweight (position, size) descriptors, and take_blobs() returns lazy file-like handles supporting byte-range reads — locally or over S3. torchcodec decodes straight from those in-memory buffers. That's why conversion is instant, pixels are bit-exact, the dataset stays video-sized, and a shuffled DataLoader gets frame-level random access anyway.

Takeaways

For a robotics team on LeRobot today: keep recording exactly as you do, run one conversion command, swap one launcher file — and get a 2.4× faster dataloader on equal-sized storage, GPUs that spend watts on matmuls instead of idling, S3 streaming, and a training table that doubles as your search index and curation surface. The model comes out statistically identical. Your wall-clock, your energy bill, and your data workflows don't.

Repro: every script, figure, and number in this post lives in lancedb/training — examples/lerobot-lancedb-libero. Datasets: HuggingFaceVLA/libero · plugin: lerobot-lancedb · hardware: 4×H100, 104 cores.
